qs.q: A child develops Lyme arthritis in the right knee months after a tick bite. Which histological feature is characteristic of the chronic synovitis seen in late Lyme arthritis?
o: Obliterative endarteritis with CD4+ T cells
Caseating granulomas with giant cell foci
qs.e: The histology of chronic Lyme arthritis characteristically shows synoviocyte hyperplasia, fibrin deposition, mononuclear cell infiltrates rich in CD4+ T cells, and obliterative endarteritis. Needle-shaped crystals are a classic feature of gout, not Lyme arthritis.

qs.q: During the evaluation of a patient with suspected Lyme arthritis, two-tier serologic testing is performed. Which test combination is recommended for diagnosis?
o: Joint aspiration followed by Gram stain
qs.e: Serologic detection of anti-Borrelia antibodies using a two-tier approach of ELISA confirmed by Western blot is the recommended diagnostic method for Lyme arthritis. Ziehl-Neelsen staining is used for mycobacterial infections like tuberculosis.

faq.a: Yes, a minority develop persistent synovitis despite antibiotics, often requiring prolonged oral therapy or referral to rheumatology.
It helps exclude infection and can relieve pain, but does not treat the underlying Borrelia infection.
Steroids suppress inflammation but do not eradicate Borrelia; they may worsen infection if given without antibiotics.

exam: What is the most appropriate next step for a patient with a swollen knee, a history of tick bite 3 months ago, and a negative Gram stain? — Perform two‑tier serology for Borrelia and start doxycycline if positive.

How does Lyme arthritis differ from septic arthritis on synovial fluid analysis? — Lyme shows sterile, inflammatory fluid with modest WBC; septic arthritis shows purulent fluid with high WBC and positive culture.

A patient with persistent knee swelling after 4 weeks of doxycycline raises what concern? — Consider chronic Lyme arthritis or an alternative diagnosis; obtain repeat serology and consider IV ceftriaxone.

Why is doxycycline preferred over amoxicillin for most adults with Lyme arthritis? — Doxycycline has better tissue penetration and covers possible co‑infection with Anaplasma; amoxicillin is less effective for joint involvement.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate cardiac evaluation in a patient with Lyme disease? — New‑onset atrioventricular block or other conduction abnormalities.
Explain why a negative PCR does not rule out Lyme arthritis. — PCR sensitivity in synovial fluid is low; diagnosis relies on serology and clinical pattern.

How would you differentiate reactive arthritis from Lyme arthritis in a patient from a low‑resource setting? — Reactive arthritis follows GI/genitourinary infection, often HLA‑B27 positive, and lacks Borrelia serology; Lyme arthritis follows tick exposure and has positive Borrelia IgG.

What preventive advice should you give to a rural worker after treating Lyme arthritis? — Use permethrin‑treated clothing, apply DEET repellent, perform daily tick checks, and avoid walking through tall grass.
ai.title: Lyme Arthritis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Lyme arthritis is a late manifestation of Borrelia burgdorferi infection, presenting as intermittent mono‑ or oligo‑arthritis of large joints. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and serology, with management focused on antibiotics and joint care.

b: Intermittent swelling of one or a few large joints, most often the knee.
Synovial fluid may show mild neutrophilia; spirochetes are rarely seen.
Two‑tier serology (ELISA followed by Western blot) is the standard diagnostic test.
sections.p: Lyme arthritis is the articular manifestation of disseminated Lyme disease, typically occurring months after a tick bite when the infection spreads to synovial tissue.

t.b: Does the patient have antibodies to Borrelia? Positive IgG confirms late infection; a negative test makes Lyme arthritis unlikely.
Is there an alternative cause (septic, crystal) for the effusion? Sterile, inflammatory fluid supports Lyme arthritis; culture or crystal analysis rules out other etiologies.
Detects spirochetal DNA in synovial fluid; positive result confirms diagnosis but low sensitivity, so a negative test does not exclude disease.

b: Stage 1 – Early localized: erythema migrans.
Stage 2 – Early disseminated: neurologic, cardiac involvement.
Stage 3 – Late disseminated: arthritis, chronic musculoskeletal pain.
sections.p: Lyme disease progresses through three clinical stages; arthritis belongs to the late disseminated stage.

b: Borrelia burgdorferi infection (most common).
Co‑infection with other tick‑borne pathogens (e.g., Anaplasma) can modify presentation.
Concurrent HIV or malaria may blunt serologic responses.
sections.p: The sole causative organism is Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by Ixodes ticks. In low‑resource settings, co‑existing infections must be considered.

b: Joint pain lasting days to weeks, resolving spontaneously, then recurring.
Absence of purulent discharge; skin over joint may be normal.
History of tick exposure or erythema migrans months earlier.
sections.p: Patients report episodic swelling, warmth, and limited movement of a large joint, often the knee, without systemic fever.
Focus on confirming Borrelia infection and excluding other causes of inflammatory arthritis.

t.b: Is there serologic evidence of infection? Positive IgG indicates late disease; IgM is usually negative at this stage.
Does the pattern meet CDC criteria? Presence of ≥2 specific IgG bands confirms Lyme arthritis.
Is the effusion inflammatory but sterile? WBC 10‑30 ×10⁹/L, neutrophil predominance, negative Gram stain and culture.
Detects DNA; positive result strengthens diagnosis, but a negative result does not rule it out.
Rely on history of tick bite, characteristic joint pattern, and exclusion of septic arthritis; treat empirically if suspicion high.

b: Persistent swelling > 6 months despite antibiotics → consider chronic Lyme arthritis or co‑existing rheumatic disease.
Concurrent cardiac (AV block) or neurologic (facial palsy) symptoms indicate disseminated disease needing urgent care.
Septic arthritis masquerading as Lyme arthritis – must be excluded promptly.
sections.p: Although usually self‑limited with treatment, untreated disease can cause persistent joint damage and rare systemic sequelae.

b: If doxycycline contraindicated or severe joint disease, use IV ceftriaxone for 14‑28 days.
Avoid long‑term NSAIDs alone; they do not treat the infection.
Physical therapy after inflammation subsides to restore range of motion.
sections.p: Antibiotic therapy eradicates the spirochete; supportive measures relieve joint symptoms.

b: Clinical review 4‑6 weeks post‑therapy; repeat serology only if symptoms persist.
Encourage use of insect repellent, long sleeves, and tick checks after outdoor exposure.
Vaccination against Lyme disease is not available; prevention relies on vector control.
sections.p: Re‑evaluate joint status after completion of antibiotics; educate on tick avoidance.

b: Rheumatoid arthritis – symmetric small‑joint involvement, rheumatoid factor positive.
Septic arthritis – acute severe pain, fever, purulent synovial fluid.
Reactive arthritis – follows gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, HLA‑B27 positive.
sections.p: Several other inflammatory arthritides mimic Lyme arthritis.

b: Early infection may yield negative IgG; rely on clinical picture.
Cross‑reactivity with other spirochetes can produce false‑positive IgM.
PCR sensitivity is low; a negative result does not exclude Lyme arthritis.
sections.p: Serologic and laboratory findings may be falsely negative or ambiguous.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging joint swelling with fever – suspect septic arthritis.
New onset cardiac block or facial palsy – indicates disseminated Lyme disease requiring urgent treatment.
